newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's CDU slams Stoiber over euro remarks.
newsitem.headline: Germany's CDU slams Stoiber over euro remarks.

text.p: A leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) attacked Bavaria state Premier Edmund Stoiber on Thursday over his threat to resist Europe's planned single currency, the euro, if entry rules were eased. Stoiber said his Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's CDU, would not tolerate any country joining European economic and monetary union (EMU) with a budget deficit above 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), fueling further a simmering row within the coalition.

But Heiner Geissler, deputy CDU/CSU parliamentary leader in the Bonn parliament, told SWF radio Stoiber was confusing mathematics with politics and making a "serious political error" that could badly damage the German economy.

"The stability of the euro does not depend on whether countries achieve 3.0. It could also be 3.1 or 3.2. There are three or four other criteria which also must be fulfilled (to qualify for EMU entry)," Geissler said.

"We must consider whether we should jeopardise the whole of European unity for the sake of a tenth of a percent. If the euro is not launched on time, then we will face a flight of investment into the deutschemark," he said.

Geissler said this would hit German imports and threaten jobs. He dismissed Stoiber's insistence on such a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria that countries wanting to launch the euro must fulfil.

"This is criteria fetishism and reminds me of the resolutions of the Marxist-Leninist wing of the Young Socialists or of the 20th party congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union," Geissler sniped in the radio interview.

When asked whether Stoiber was asking for a confrontation with Kohl, he said: "One almost has this impression. But it's not just a confrontation with Kohl, but also with the CDU". Geissler's remarks came amid signs of a widening rift between the centre-right CDU and its right-wing sister party CSU, which has taken a more euro-sceptical stance to EMU since the new left-wing government was elected in France last month.

Several leading figures in the CSU have said they fear France will now seek to dilute the Maastricht criteria, but have denied reports of a clash between the Bavarian base of the party and its leader Finance Minister Theo Waigel on the issue.
Waigel, seemingly torn between his party and coalition partners in Bonn, has repeatedly insisted Germany will fulfil the criteria exactly and that three percent means 3.0.

Stoiber's remarks in an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily won the unlikely support of Gerhard Schroeder, the left-leaning Social Democrat premier of Lower Saxony, who polls show could beat Kohl in the 1998 elections.

But Kohl's other junior coalition partner criticised Stoiber for "euro-populism", arguing that ahead of Bavarian state elections he was playing on Germans' fears about swapping their beloved mark for a potentially softer currency.
Opinion polls regularly show about two-thirds of the German population are opposed to trading in their marks for euros.
Geissler said that despite the row between CDU and CSU coalition partners the coalition was not near collapse.

"This (talk) makes people and business uncertain. They and German banks are prepared mentally for a switch to the euro but when this is constantly questioned it hampers a regeneration of the jobs market, which we urgently need," he said.
"We must put a stop to this fundamentalism," he said.
